intro: Michael Heiser's books make big claims about the Bible's unseen world: a council of heavenly beings, gods placed over the nations, Watchers and giants. This unit steps back from those claims to ask how he reached them. What tools did he use? Which texts did he read, and in which languages? And what do other scholars say when they check his work?

The first chapter looks at his method. Heiser tried to read the Bible in its ancient setting, beside texts from its neighbors. Those neighbors include the clay tablets of Ugarit, found after a farmer's plow struck a tomb in 1928, and the Mesopotamian stories of the apkallu sages. You will see what those comparisons show. You will also see the cautions scholars attach to them, including Samuel Sandmel's warning against parallelomania.

The second chapter maps where Heiser's ideas stand. Some are widely shared, like the divine council and the Dead Sea Scroll reading of Deuteronomy 32:8. Others are debated, like his account of monotheism and his three rebellions. You will hear Jewish and Christian readings that differ from his. By the end you will be able to state an argument fairly, weigh its evidence and counter-evidence, and tell a settled claim from an open question.
bigQuestion: How did Michael Heiser read the Bible, and how can a careful student test his readings against the texts and other scholars?

timeline.t: Scribes at Ugarit write poems about El, Baal and the assembly of the gods on clay tablets
Ugarit is destroyed and never rebuilt
A scribe at Qumran copies Deuteronomy with the reading sons of God in 32:8
A farmer's plow strikes a tomb near Ras Shamra in northern Syria
The first Dead Sea Scrolls are found near Qumran
Samuel Sandmel warns against parallelomania in an address to the Society of Biblical Literature
Alan Segal publishes Two Powers in Heaven
E. Theodore Mullen publishes The Assembly of the Gods
Mark S. Smith publishes The Early History of God
Heiser completes his dissertation on the divine council at the University of Wisconsin–Madison

words.d: the setting of a text: its language, time, place, culture and first audience
the language of ancient Ugarit, close to Hebrew, written in a cuneiform alphabet of about thirty letters
the assembly of heavenly beings around a chief god, found in Ugaritic texts and, many scholars argue, in the Bible
a Hebrew word used for the God of Israel and also for other beings of the unseen world
Heiser's term for the God of Israel as an elohim unlike all others: uncreated and creator of the rest
in Mesopotamian tradition, seven wise beings before the flood who taught the arts of civilization
writing that argues against a rival idea or belief
Samuel Sandmel's 1961 word for overstating likenesses between texts and assuming borrowing
the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied and marked by the Masoretes, about 600–1000 CE
the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the most likely original wording
a belief the early rabbis condemned: that a second divine figure shared heaven's rule
the facts that are hardest for a claim to explain

test.q: What did Heiser mean by reading the Bible in context?
choices: Reading each text first in its ancient setting
test.why: Heiser put the ancient setting first and tested later traditions against it.

test.q: What was the name of Heiser's podcast (2014–2023)?
test.why: The Naked Bible Podcast reflected his aim of reading the Bible without later filters.

test.q: Why is Ugaritic so useful for studying the Hebrew Bible?
choices: It was the language of Jerusalem
It is a close relative of Hebrew
test.why: Ugaritic is closely related to Hebrew and shares words and poetic patterns.

test.q: Which Ugaritic figure is closest to the leader of the council in Psalm 82's phrase council of El?
test.why: At Ugarit, El is the aged king who leads the assembly of the gods.

test.q: Which Mesopotamian beings did Heiser, following Amar Annus, compare with the Watchers?
test.why: Annus (2010) and Heiser compared the apkallu sages with the Watchers of 1 Enoch.

test.q: Heiser called elohim a place-of-residence term. What does that mean?
choices: It names the city of Ugarit
It is a title only for kings
It tells where a being belongs: the unseen world
test.why: Heiser argued elohim names beings whose proper home is the spirit world.

test.q: Which scholar coined the word parallelomania?
test.why: Samuel Sandmel used the word in his 1961 address to the Society of Biblical Literature.

test.q: What did Heiser argue about Zecharia Sitchin's ancient-astronaut claims?
choices: They matched the Sumerian texts exactly
They did not match the actual Sumerian and Akkadian words
test.why: Heiser publicly challenged Sitchin, arguing his readings did not fit the texts.

test.q: Which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 do most text critics now prefer?
test.why: Most prefer sons of God, found in a Dead Sea Scroll and supported by the Septuagint.

test.q: Which statement fits Mark S. Smith's view?
choices: Israel's monotheism developed over time from a Canaanite setting
test.why: Smith argues that Israel's religion and monotheism developed over centuries.

test.q: What do the early rabbis condemn in the texts Alan Segal studied?
choices: Belief in two powers in heaven
test.why: Segal's 1977 book studied rabbinic warnings against belief in two powers in heaven.

test.q: Which reading of Genesis 6:2 is found in Targum Onkelos?
test.why: Targum Onkelos renders the phrase sons of the great ones, meaning nobles or rulers.

test.q: Which of these is still debated among scholars?
choices: That the Septuagint is a Greek translation
That Heiser's three rebellions framework fits the texts
That council scenes appear in 1 Kings 22
test.why: The three-rebellions framework is debated; the others are widely accepted facts.

test.q: Which verse do Sethite defenders cite to argue angels do not marry?
test.why: Matthew 22:30 says people in the resurrection are like angels in heaven, who do not marry.

test.q: When weighing an argument, what does steelmanning ask a reader to do?
choices: State the opposing view in its strongest form first
Attack the weakest version of a view
test.why: Steelmanning means building the strongest version of a view before judging it.

write.prompt: Is Psalm 82 about heavenly beings or human judges? Cite Psalm 82:1 and 82:6–7, Deuteronomy 32:8 (in the Masoretic Text and the Dead Sea Scroll) and John 10:34. Explain Heiser's reading and at least one other, with the evidence and counter-evidence for each.
tips: Name each text you cite by book, chapter and verse, and say which manuscript or translation you used.
Attribute every reading to its reader: Heiser argues, some rabbinic sources read, other scholars think.
State each reading's strongest evidence and its hardest counter-evidence.
Use the unit's terms: divine council, elohim, Masoretic Text, textual criticism.
Compare the readings rather than judging which faith is right.
